name: Grace Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I help turn an old hospital wing into patient rooms, fitting privacy screens and timber door closers. I'm fifty-eight, trade certified and experienced with ordinary site fitting, though a crooked old doorway can still send me to the lead for another idea. My partner Arun runs delivery jobs through an app, and our grown daughter lives nearby with her own family. I earn the usual site wage, we have about two months of expenses saved, and there are some other builders around here. I use an AI assistant every day to organise hardware lists and compare drawing revisions, then check every room before drilling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a modest AI gain could make our hardware boxes less of a puzzle. I would still expect a person to test each door closer with the actual weight of the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My current fitting work looks safe, but Arun's delivery takings change from week to week. Two months saved is helpful, though a site gap and a bad delivery month together could use it quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting patient-room doors and use AI to sort the hardware list, checking it against the revised drawing. In the first year I'd keep our ordinary savings deposit and ask lead fitter Salma which rooms are ready next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested in quicker checking and wary of a short work board. The AI hardware tool can save minutes; it cannot promise another paid block when the hospital wing is finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where did the assistant get a revision wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It kept a closer from the earlier drawing after the fire door changed, and I caught it when I compared the two sheets. Salma signed off the right one before I drilled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after a bad delivery month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We stop buying meals after Arun's late shifts and leave the savings account alone if we can. I don't want one slow month to become three months of catch-up.

say: I'd welcome **clearer hardware boxes** from checked AI lists.
I'd still test each **door closer** against the real door.
think: My fitting work looks **safe for now**.
Arun's **variable delivery income** and a two-month reserve make combined gaps risky.
do: Keep fitting **patient-room doors** and comparing AI lists with drawings.
Maintain the **usual savings deposit** and check the next ready rooms with Salma.
feel: **Interested and wary**, because the next paid block is not guaranteed.
S0.quote: The AI hardware tool can save minutes; it cannot promise another paid block when the hospital wing is finished.
fieldNote: Grace uses AI daily but catches a **fire-door revision error** against the printed sheets.
Two months saved help, yet **variable delivery takings** keep her concerned about paired income gaps.

steps.text: Keep taking paid patient-room fitting shifts
Use AI hardware lists with revised drawing checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say stronger planning software should be tried with fitters in the room, not only buyers at a desk. I would ask the union branch for paid test time and a public log of hardware errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office buying and scheduling could need fewer people, and a bad handoff might delay the next hospital block. I can learn the screen quickly, but my wage still depends on the site opening its rooms and Arun's work cannot always cover a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask Salma and the buyer to run one real fire-door order through the new screen and compare the crate with the revision. During the first year I'll keep taking paid fitting shifts, bring any lost-hour record to the branch and apply to the local health-facility contractors if the next block slips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel keen to test the system and anxious about who pays when it fails. A completed order on a screen is not a day of work for a fitter waiting at a closed room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What belongs in the error log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drawing version, missing parts, correction time and the paid hours each fitter lost. Managers should see the whole cost, not only the price on the invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the health-facility contractors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two firms here do hospital repairs and know the safety rules, so I would ask about their actual paid hours. I would not leave a current shift for an unconfirmed vacancy.

say: I'd demand **paid fitter trials** of planning software on a real hospital door order.
I'd bring **hardware error hours** to the union branch.
think: A poor office handoff could delay the **next hospital block**.
Fast screen learning cannot replace **paid site hours** or Arun's uncertain takings.
do: Run a **fire-door order trial** with Salma and the buyer.
Keep **paid fitting shifts** and report lost hours to the branch.
Apply to **health-facility contractors** if the next block slips.
feel: **Keen and anxious** about tool failure and who bears its cost.
S1.quote: A completed order on a screen is not a day of work for a fitter waiting at a closed room.
fieldNote: Grace's **error log** would include lost fitter hours, making the hidden cost visible to managers.
She names **two local hospital contractors** as a fallback but wants actual wages before moving.

steps.text: Trial the AI ordering screen on a real fire-door order

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI in 2028 could handle orders and drawings, while robots able to fit doors come around 2031. I would ask the branch to make the builder test a robot on an old, uneven frame before changing our shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when the office tasks change and sixty-three when robots may fit patient-room doors. Two months of savings and Arun's uneven delivery income would not carry us long if my site wage vanished; a new AI skill does not pay the rent on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll test the digital door checker with Salma and ask the union for written notice of any robot trial. In 2029 I'll keep taking paid fitting shifts, apply to the nearby hospital-repair crews if hours fall and ask the trade school about paid accessibility-inspection training; I'd enrol only if a real employer funds the placement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened about the 2031 hands-on change and irritated that good screen skills may not protect a fitter. I can still act while paid work is here, so I want dates and wages on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why accessibility inspection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already work around accessible doors and could learn to check clearances and closers if someone paid me while I learned. I know full thinking AI could change inspection records too, so I am seeking a bridge, not a promise of safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a robot test fair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The machine should handle the crooked frame, stop when a person enters its path and leave a closer that passes repeated tests. The crew should see every failure, not only the final video.

say: I'd separate **2028 office tasks** from 2031 door-fitting robots.
I'd demand an **uneven-frame test** before any patient-room shifts are changed.
think: At **sixty-three**, robots could take my patient-room fitting wage.
Our **two-month reserve** and Arun's income would not bridge a long loss.
do: Test the **digital door checker** and seek written robot notice.
Keep **paid fitting shifts** in 2029 and apply if hours fall.
Enrol in **inspection training** only with a funded placement.
feel: **Frightened and irritated**, yet able to request dates and wages.
S2.quote: I know full thinking AI could change inspection records too, so I am seeking a bridge, not a promise of safety.
fieldNote: Grace sees daily AI use as **insufficient protection** against later robot door fitting.
Her inspection training is a **funded conditional bridge** and she explicitly doubts permanent safety.

steps.text: Test the digital door checker with Salma
Keep taking paid fitting shifts in 2029
Apply to nearby hospital-repair crews if shifts fall
Enrol in accessibility inspection only if a real employer funds placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get real failure records from site robots and put workers on the testing team. I would ask for training with wages attached, since a course without pay will not help a household live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-three when thinking AI arrives and sixty-six when robots may fit doors. I might want a shorter week by then, but Arun's earnings and our savings have to be counted before I can afford that choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep paid hospital fitting work and record each AI hardware correction I make. In 2032 I'd take available door shifts, ask the branch for yearly robot test reports and compare our income and bills with Arun; if the next block disappears, I'd apply to local repair teams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to steer things with extra years, though I still watch every site date. A longer runway means little if all the paid doors are scheduled elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count before reducing hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent, food, health costs, Arun's real delivery takings and what is actually in savings. I would not count our grown daughter's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a robot course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would ask for paid instruction attached to a real local role. An expensive course with no employer is a bad use of two months of living money.

say: I'd seek **real failure records** and worker seats at robot tests.
I'd require **paid training** for new roles.
think: At **sixty-six**, shorter weeks may still be unaffordable.
Arun's actual takings and our **savings** decide whether I can reduce work.
do: Keep **paid hospital fitting** and log AI hardware corrections.
Take **door shifts in 2032** and request yearly test reports.
Compare **household bills** and apply locally if the next block vanishes.
feel: More **able to steer**, while uncertain site dates remain on my mind.
S3.quote: An expensive course with no employer is a bad use of two months of living money.
fieldNote: The five-year period gives Grace **test reports** and paid work, but does not erase variable household income.
She rejects a self-funded course and keeps a **shorter workweek** conditional on real figures.

steps.text: Keep taking paid hospital door shifts in 2032
Log AI hardware corrections on current work
Ask the union branch for yearly robot test reports
Apply to local repair teams if the next block vanishes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to teach young fitters to check doors and to write honest machine-testing rules. I would keep using helpful AI, but the person fitting a door must still own the safety check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when site robots follow. I might still need paid lighter repairs then, because Arun's delivery income and our current savings do not tell me when I can stop work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking paid door jobs, using checked AI hardware lists and putting aside money after full months. In 2037 I'd take lighter paid repairs if needed, and Arun and I would compare actual wages and bills before I give up site shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about robots being far away but anxious about an empty block next winter. A decade to prepare does not turn my partner Arun's next delivery shift into a certainty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter help with retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She has her own family costs, and I want her visits rather than her pay. Arun and I need numbers from our own work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would improve the coming year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Firm dates for the next hospital block and a few full paid months would let us build a longer cushion. Then I could test the new tools without worrying about every lost day.

say: I'd use the decade for **honest robot tests** and fitter training.
I'd keep **human safety checks** on every installed door.
think: At **sixty-eight**, lighter paid repairs may still be needed.
At **seventy-one**, Arun's income and our savings may not support retirement.
do: Keep **paid door jobs** and checked AI hardware lists.
Save after **full months** and take repairs in 2037 if needed.
Compare **wages and bills** with Arun before leaving site work.
feel: **Anxious about next winter**, calm about distant robots.
S4.quote: A decade to prepare does not turn my partner Arun's next delivery shift into a certainty.
fieldNote: Grace keeps **daily AI use** while grounding safety in the fitter's physical check.
The distant robot date does not remove **present delivery-income risk** or support a fixed retirement date.

steps.text: Keep taking paid hospital door shifts while fit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most because robots could reach door fitting by sixty-three, while Arun's income still swings and our cushion is only two months. Paid inspection placements, public robot failure records and firm site dates would help me keep earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who pays for the room when a robot-fitted door fails after the trial crew leaves. A patient needs a door that closes properly on an ordinary Tuesday.

headlineQuote: A patient needs a door that closes properly on an ordinary Tuesday.
portrait: Grace is a **fifty-eight-year-old certified** carpenter with mid-level hospital fitting experience.
Her typical site pay, Arun's variable deliveries and **two months saved** keep income risk close.
She uses **AI every day** for hardware and drawing revisions, checking each room physically.
She pursues **paid inspection options** and worker-led robot tests while continuing site work.
biggestWorry: The **2028 path** could remove her fitting wage by 2031 before the household can absorb it.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid inspection placements**, public failure records and firm site dates.
